name: Nine-Tailed Fox
description: A powerful fox spirit of East Asian mythology, distinguished by nine tails. It can live for centuries, accumulate spiritual power, and shapeshift into a beautiful human — beneficent in early Chinese tradition, often seductive and dangerous in later accounts.
full_description: The nine-tailed fox (Chinese 九尾狐 jiǔwěihú; Korean 구미호 gumiho; Japanese 九尾の狐 kyūbi no kitsune; Vietnamese hồ ly tinh) is one of the most influential supernatural figures of East Asian mythology. The earliest reference appears in the Shanhaijing (Classic of Mountains and Seas), which describes a nine-tailed fox in the land of Qingqiu (青丘). In early Chinese tradition the nine-tailed fox was an auspicious omen associated with rulership and harmony; later, particularly from the Han onwards, it shifted toward an ambivalent and then frequently malevolent figure — a spiritually advanced fox capable of shapeshifting into a beautiful woman to bewitch and harm men. Scholar Guo Pu (276–324 CE) systematised the idea that foxes acquire transformative powers with age (50, 100, 1000 years), and the celestial nine-tailed fox is described in the Tang-dynasty Youyang Zazu as serving in the Palace of the Sun and Moon. Korean tradition (gumiho) typically frames the nine-tailed fox as a dangerous female spirit, while modern Japanese tradition incorporates the kitsune complex and the Tamamo-no-Mae legend. The figure remains massively present in contemporary East Asian and global popular culture.
origin: East Asia: China, Korea, Japan, and Vietnam.

etymology.meaning: Literally 'nine-tailed fox'; tails accumulate with age and spiritual cultivation
etymology.first_use: Shanhaijing (Classic of Mountains and Seas), pre-Han China

timeline.event: Shanhaijing locates the nine-tailed fox in the land of Qingqiu
Birth of Guo Pu (276–324 CE), who would systematise fox-spirit transformation theory
timeline.significance: Anchors the canonical scheme of fox transformation by age (50/100/1000 years)
timeline.source: Wikipedia, 'Nine-tailed fox'; classical biographies of Guo Pu

timeline.event: Compilation of the Tang-dynasty Youyang Zazu (c. 863 CE) with its description of celestial nine-tailed foxes serving in the Palace of the Sun and Moon
timeline.significance: Major Tang-era systematisation of nine-tailed fox lore

related.name: Kitsune
related.description: Japanese fox spirit complex of which the nine-tailed kyūbi no kitsune is the most powerful form

related.name: Huli jing
related.description: Chinese fox spirit class; the nine-tailed fox is its highest form

cultural_notes: The nine-tailed fox is variously seen as auspicious omen, dangerous seductress, demonic temptress, and celestial servant, depending on tradition and era.
